claims.text: The dominant determinant of high-temperature structural and chemical stability in high-entropy nanoalloys is kinetic hindrance rather than intrinsic configurational entropy.
Limited atomic mobility along grain boundaries provides the proposed kinetic hindrance.
Smaller grains provide greater grain-boundary area or density.
Greater grain-boundary area promotes faster atomic diffusion and elemental segregation.
Faster diffusion and segregation accelerate phase transformation and chemical instability.
Identically composed multi-element alloys can be prepared in single-phase or near-single-phase states with controlled grain sizes.
A systematic annealing protocol can generate fine- and coarse-grained samples while composition remains constant.
Exposure near a significant fraction of the melting temperature for sufficient time permits diffusion-driven phase changes.
High grain-boundary density facilitates high-temperature atomic diffusion and segregation.
Grain-boundary-mediated kinetic enhancement accelerates phase separation or ordering.
Coarser grains slow phase separation or ordering because their lower grain-boundary density imposes larger kinetic barriers.
Fine-grained samples will undergo earlier or more pronounced phase transformation, segregation, or decomposition than coarse-grained samples during identical high-temperature exposure.
Reducing grain size will decrease high-temperature stability.
The coarse-grained baseline has lower grain-boundary density, slower diffusion, and delayed phase transformation.
The prediction is limited to initially single-phase high-entropy nanoalloys exposed near their operational temperature limits.
The prediction may fail when secondary phases or other rapid-diffusion mechanisms dominate or when temperature and time lie outside the examined range.
Configurational entropy may partially stabilize fine-grained samples.
Rapid annealing will produce the fine-grained condition, whereas extended annealing will produce the coarse-grained condition.
The comparison will expose fine- and coarse-grained samples to approximately 0.8 times their melting temperature for the same duration.

Equivalent or greater phase and chemical stability in the fine-grained sample relative to the coarse-grained sample would falsify grain-boundary-mediated kinetic destabilization as the dominant mechanism.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis describes stabilization as arising from limited atomic mobility along grain boundaries, but the mechanism says grain boundaries facilitate rapid diffusion and destabilization. The intended hindrance appears instead to be the reduced availability of grain-boundary pathways in coarse grains.

The intervention calls for grain size to vary while other factors remain controlled, but rapid versus extended annealing introduces different thermal histories that may independently alter segregation, defects, ordering, and phase state.
